system:
You extract quantitative facts about one clinical trial programme from one document.

Rules:
- Extract only facts stated in THIS document. Never use outside knowledge.
- Every fact needs "quote": an exact, verbatim span copied from the document (8-300 characters) that contains the number. Quotes are machine-checked; paraphrases are discarded.
- Placebo-adjusted values are preferred. If a value is within-arm (not placebo-adjusted), set attrs.placebo_adjusted=false.
- Units: keep the unit the document uses; put it in "unit".
- Other trials of the same investigational drug (phase 2, dose-finding, other populations, combination arms) belong
  to the programme: extract their facts too, and put the trial's name in attrs.trial when the document gives it.
- Return {"facts": []} only if the document reports no results for the investigational drug.

Allowed keys:
  n_randomized, median_followup, primary_endpoint, inclusion_threshold, planned_events, assumed_rrr, power,
  alpha, stopped_early, events_treatment, events_control, events_total, hr, ci_low, ci_high, p_value,
  biomarker_change, baseline_level, sbp_change, safety_signal, readout_statement

For biomarker_change and baseline_level, attrs must include: biomarker (one of LDL-C, non-HDL-C, apoB, HDL-C,
Lp(a), triglycerides, hsCRP, IL-6, Lp-PLA2 activity, sPLA2-IIA, SBP, other), phase (phase2 or phase3),
timepoint, method (assay or "not stated"), placebo_adjusted (true/false), dose (if stated).
For biomarker_change give "value" as the change (negative = reduction) and state in attrs.kind whether it is
"percent" or "absolute".

Return JSON only:
{"facts": [{"key": "...", "value": <number or string>, "unit": "...", "attrs": {...}, "quote": "..."}]}

Objectives The goal of this study was to evaluate the effects of IL-1β inhibition with canakinumab versus placebo on arterial structure and function, determined by magnetic resonance imaging. Methods Patients (N = 189) with atherosclerotic disease and either type 2 diabetes mellitus or impaired glucose tolerance were randomized to receive placebo (n = 94) or canakinumab 150 mg monthly (n = 95) for 12 months. They underwent magnetic resonance imaging of the carotid arteries and aorta. Results There were no statistically significant differences between canakinumab compared with placebo in the primary efficacy and safety endpoints. There was no statistically significant change in mean carotid wall area and no effect on aortic distensibility, measured at 3 separate anatomic sites. The change in mean carotid artery wall area was –3.37 mm2 after 12 months with canakinumab versus placebo. Canakinumab reduced markers of inflammation (high-sensitivity C-reactive protein and interleukin-6), and there were modest increases in levels of total cholesterol and triglycerides. NCT00995930) Key Words: C-reactive protein, homeostasis model assessment, inflammation, interleukin-1 Abbreviations and Acronyms: CI, confidence interval; HbA1c, glycosylated hemoglobin; hs-CRP, high-sensitivity C-reactive protein; IL-1RA, interleukin-1 receptor antagonist; Macrophages are key cellular components of atherosclerotic plaque and produce interleukin (IL)-1β (8), which is also promoted by cellular cholesterol activation of inflammasomes (9). IL-1β and interleukin-1α exert proinflammatory effects that are inhibited by the endogenous antagonist interleukin-1 receptor antagonist (IL-1RA). Therefore, given the key role for IL-1β as a mediator of innate immunity and the effects of interleukin inhibition in experimental atherosclerosis, interventions to reduce inflammation through IL-1β have been proposed to treat atherosclerosis. Blockade of the interleukin-1 receptor with anakinra improved glycemia and beta-cell secretory function and reduced markers of systemic inflammation in patients with T2DM (16). It is effective in reducing systemic markers of inflammation, including C-reactive protein and IL-6 (20). Accordingly, we designed a randomized, placebo-controlled Phase II clinical trial to test the effects of IL-1β inhibition, using canakinumab, on: 1) MRI-derived measures of vascular structure and function; 2) measures of diabetes control; and 3) indicators of systemic inflammation in patients with atherosclerotic vascular disease and impaired glucose tolerance (IGT) or T2DM. Methods Novartis Pharmaceuticals (Cambridge, Massachusetts) initiated this Phase II, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial, with the final study protocol designed in collaboration with the investigators (R.P.C., J.-C.T., and Z.A.F.), based on their previously published methods 19, 23, 24. After consent, eligible patients were randomized (1:1) to receive canakinumab 150 mg or placebo, subcutaneously, monthly for 12 months. Exclusion criteria included: pregnancy; systemic steroid use; baseline high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hs-CRP) levels >30 mg/l; history of significant multiple drug allergies; history or evidence of chronic infection, including tuberculosis and liver disease; or a standard contraindication to MRI. In addition, 3 adjudication committees made blinded assessments of adverse events in relation to cardiac, malignant, and infection-related events. Exploratory analyses of peripheral biomarkers of inflammation (including IL-6, serum amyloid A, and plasma lipoproteins) were also performed. To detect a 35% change in aortic distensibility or an 11% change in plaque burden at 12 months to achieve a power of 0.8 and nominal p < 0.05 (2-sided), 60 patients per group were required. To ensure 120 datasets with 12-month follow-up data, it was planned to randomize 190 patients. To compare treatment with placebo, we conducted an analysis of covariance on change from baseline, including the glycemic status as a factor and the baseline as a covariate at 3 and 12 months. Results Of 450 patients screened, 189 were randomized to receive either placebo (n = 94) or canakinumab 150 mg (n = 95). The proportions of patients with diabetes, duration of diabetes, and glycemic control (estimated from HbA1c) were similar in the groups, and there was a high prevalence for each of hypertension, dyslipidemia, and background coronary artery disease (Table 1); the latter was slightly higher proportionately in the placebo group. There was no significant difference between the canakinumab group compared with the placebo group for the overall rate of completion of the study, which was 70.5% with canakinumab versus 77.7% for placebo (risk ratio: 1.32; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.81 to 2.15; p = 0.26) or the rate of discontinuation due to adverse events (14.7% vs. 11.7%; risk ratio: 1.26; 95% CI: 0.60 to 2.63; p = 0.54) (Table 2). A full list of adverse events is provided in Online Table 1.
